brain-tumour.name: Brain tumours
brain-tumour.definition: A brain tumour is a growth of abnormal cells in or around the brain, and it may be non-cancerous or cancerous.
brain-tumour.overview: Brain tumours can be non-cancerous (benign) or cancerous (malignant). Some start in the brain, while others start elsewhere in the body and spread to it. The symptoms depend mainly on where the tumour is and how big it is. Treatment depends on the type, size, position and grade of the tumour and may involve surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy or careful monitoring. The outlook varies a great deal from one type to another.
causes: The NHS says the risk of a brain tumour rises with age, although some types are more common in children
Exposure to radiation is a known risk factor, but the NHS says it accounts for only a very small number of tumours
Inherited conditions such as neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2 are linked to a higher risk
riskFactors: Radiation exposure, including earlier radiotherapy to the head
signs: Weakness on one side of the body
Changes in memory, mood or personality
complications: Raised pressure inside the skull, causing headaches, nausea and vomiting
Problems with balance, movement, speech or vision, depending on the area affected
brain-tumour.diagnosis: Diagnosis usually involves a neurological examination, a brain scan and often a biopsy to confirm the type of tumour. The NHS says a brain scan, usually an MRI, is the main test. Brain tumours are given a grade from 1 to 4, with grades 1 and 2 generally low grade and grades 3 and 4 high grade.
brain-tumour.treatment: Treatment depends on the type, size, position and grade of the tumour, any biomarkers and the symptoms it causes. Options include watchful waiting, surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and targeted therapy, and many people have a combination. Medicines can help with symptoms, such as steroids for swelling and anti-seizure medicines for fits.
brain-tumour.prevention: Radiation exposure is a known risk factor, but the NHS says it accounts for only a very small number of brain tumours. The sources retrieved do not describe a reliable way to prevent most brain tumours.
brain-tumour.seekCare: The NHS advises seeing a GP for a headache that feels different from the usual kind, or for headaches that are getting worse. Persistent or worsening symptoms such as seizures, vision changes or personality changes also need a medical assessment. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a first-time fit, a fit lasting longer than usual for that person, or a sudden, extremely painful headache.

sections.heading: What is a brain tumour?
sections.body:
A brain tumour is a growth of abnormal cells in or around the brain. Brain tumours can be non-cancerous (benign) or cancerous (malignant), and the NHS notes that non-cancerous tumours tend to grow slowly. Tumours that start in the brain are called primary tumours, while others start elsewhere in the body and spread to the brain. Common primary types include gliomas, which develop from glial cells that support nerve cells, and meningiomas, which arise from the membranes around the brain and spinal cord.

Glioblastoma is the highest-grade type of astrocytoma, which is a kind of glioma, and is among the most aggressive primary brain tumours. Meningiomas are grouped into three WHO grades, and grade 1 is the most common and typically slow growing.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a brain tumour?
sections.body:
Symptoms depend on which part of the brain is affected and how big the tumour is. The NHS lists headaches and seizures (fits) as common symptoms, and says they should be checked even though they may not mean a tumour. Cancer Research UK says a headache on its own is unlikely to be a brain tumour. It describes headaches with sickness, headaches that wake a person at night or come with eye problems, and headaches that get steadily worse over weeks as ones to have checked.

Other possible symptoms include weakness on one side of the body, memory or personality changes, and problems with speech or vision. Raised pressure inside the skull can cause nausea and vomiting, and symptoms can also include tiredness, mood changes and problems with movement or balance. Symptoms may come on suddenly or develop slowly over months or years, according to the NHS.

sections.heading: What causes brain tumours?
sections.body:
For most brain tumours the sources retrieved do not point to a clear single cause. The NHS says the risk rises with age, although some types are more common in children. Radiation is a known risk factor, but the NHS says it accounts for only a very small number of tumours. Research summarised by Cancer Research UK links radiation in childhood most strongly to meningioma, and radiotherapy for an earlier brain tumour to a higher chance of a second one.

The National Cancer Institute lists inherited conditions such as neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2 as risk factors. Even in these conditions it remains hard to predict which people will develop a tumour. Age and sex also appear to influence the risk of meningioma, with grade 1 tumours more common in women and higher grades more common in men.

sections.heading: How is a brain tumour diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP asks about symptoms and may refer the person to a specialist. Cancer Research UK sets out when urgent referral is advised, and the thresholds differ for adults, for people under 25 and between the nations of the UK. For children, it says the GP should consider referring to a specialist within 48 hours if there is concern about brain or nervous system function.

Diagnosis usually includes a neurological examination, a brain scan and often a biopsy, which is a sample of tumour tissue, to confirm the type. The NHS says a brain scan, usually an MRI, is the main test. Tumours are then given a grade from 1 to 4, and grades 1 and 2 are generally called low grade while grades 3 and 4 are called high grade.

sections.heading: How are brain tumours treated?
sections.body:
Macmillan says treatment depends on the type of tumour, its size, position and grade, any biomarkers and the symptoms. Options include watchful waiting, surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and targeted therapy, and many people have a combination. The NHS says surgery is the main treatment for most types of malignant brain tumour. Where a tumour cannot be removed completely, taking out part of it can still help.

Brain Tumour Research says radiotherapy can cure some small, non-cancerous or very slow-growing low-grade tumours. For more aggressive tumours it is more likely to shrink the tumour or halt its growth for a time. Chemotherapy is often given after surgery or alongside radiotherapy. Non-cancerous tumours often respond well to treatment, and the NHS says treatment may not be needed straight away because they tend to grow slowly. Medicines such as steroids for swelling, anti-seizure medicines and painkillers for headaches can help control symptoms.

sections.heading: What is the outlook, and what about daily life?
sections.body:
The outlook varies a great deal and depends on the type of tumour, where it is in the brain and how well treatment works. Because brain tumours are uncommon and varied, the outlook is hard to predict for an individual. Treatment of non-cancerous tumours is often successful, and a full recovery is possible.

A 2024 review describes treatment as often combining surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy with intensive rehabilitation. GOV.UK says a person with a brain tumour must tell the DVLA, and that the rules depend on the type of tumour, where it is and the treatment given. The clinical team or the DVLA can confirm what applies in a particular case.

faqs.q: Is a headache a sign of a brain tumour?
faqs.a: Cancer Research UK says a headache on its own is unlikely to be a brain tumour. It advises seeing a doctor about headaches that come with sickness, wake a person at night, come with eye problems or get steadily worse over weeks. The NHS suggests seeing a GP about a headache that feels different from the usual kind or is getting worse.

No, brain tumours can be non-cancerous (benign) or cancerous (malignant). The NHS says non-cancerous tumours tend to grow slowly and often respond well to treatment. Tumours are also given a grade from 1 to 4, which the NHS says is generally low grade for 1 and 2 and high grade for 3 and 4.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a glioma, a glioblastoma and a meningioma?
faqs.a: Gliomas develop from glial cells, which support nerve cells in the brain. Glioblastoma is the highest-grade type of astrocytoma, one kind of glioma, and is among the most aggressive primary brain tumours. Meningiomas arise from the membranes around the brain and spinal cord, and most are grade 1 and slow growing.

faqs.q: Can a brain tumour be cured?
faqs.a: It depends on the type. Treatment of non-cancerous tumours is often successful, and Brain Tumour Research says radiotherapy can cure some small, non-cancerous or very slow-growing tumours. For more aggressive tumours, radiotherapy is more likely to shrink the tumour or halt its growth for a time.

faqs.q: Do people with a brain tumour have to tell the DVLA?
faqs.a: GOV.UK says a person with a brain tumour must tell the DVLA. How long driving must stop depends on the type of tumour, where it is in the brain and the treatment given. The GOV.UK guidance is the authority, and the clinical team or the DVLA can confirm what applies.

faqs.q: When is a seizure an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if someone has a fit for the first time or a fit that lasts longer than usual for them. A sudden, extremely painful headache is also a reason for 999 or A&E. Cancer Research UK says anyone who has a seizure should see a doctor or go to A&E straight away.

keyFacts.label: Main types
keyFacts.value: Gliomas, meningiomas, pituitary tumours, and tumours that spread to the brain from elsewhere

keyFacts.label: Common symptoms
keyFacts.value: Headaches, seizures (fits), and changes in vision, speech, memory or personality

keyFacts.label: Main test
keyFacts.value: A brain scan, usually MRI, and often a biopsy

keyFacts.label: Grading
keyFacts.value: Grades 1 to 4; 1 and 2 are generally low grade, 3 and 4 high grade

keyFacts.label: Main treatments
keyFacts.value: Surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapy or watchful waiting, plus medicines for symptoms
